title: TensorRT / Triton / Custom-kernel integration experiments and tradeoffs
content:
Purpose

This doc captures experiment notes, microbenchmarks, and tradeoffs for integrating TensorRT, NVIDIA Triton, and our own custom kernels into Redwood's serving runtime. Goal is to decide recommended integration patterns for low-latency single-stream requests and high-throughput batching use cases while preserving KV-cache correctness for chat-style workloads. This is a working draft - contains informal notes, commands, and open questions.

Context & motivation

- We need predictable latency for realtime features (chat UI, token-by-token streaming) and high throughput for batch/embedding jobs.
- Options: use TensorRT-compiled engines (fast, memory-optimized), run through Triton Inference Server (serves multiple backends + model management), or implement/maintain custom kernels in our runtime optimized for our control flows (KV-cache friendly, fused ops).
- Key constraints: support large models (7B-70B), quantized formats (int8/4/LLM-int8), KV cache streaming (append-only decode), and per-request SLOs (p50/p95/p99).

Experiment summary (high level)

1) TensorRT standalone engines (libtorch/TensorRT bindings in our process)
- Pros: best per-token throughput for single GPU setups after conversion; fused attention kernels and kernel-level optimizations; benefits from TensorRT optimized memory layout and reduced memory overhead.
- Cons: conversion fragility across model variants and ops (custom ops require plugin dev); rebuilding engine when sequence-length or batch-shape changes; limited dynamic-shape handling historically (we tested dynamic shapes but fallback costs exist).

2) Triton in front of TensorRT (Triton+TensorRT backend)
- Pros: Triton provides model repository semantics, model versioning, concurrent model instances, HTTP/gRPC endpoints, and multi-model GPU scheduling. Easier to integrate with autoscaling and multi-tenant routing.
- Cons: extra process boundary implies serialization overhead; Triton scheduling can fight our runtime-level batching resulting in unpredictable tail latencies; less visibility/control into KV-cache memory layout - we need to marshall KV tensors across process boundary for streaming decode, which adds copy overhead unless using GPU shared memory mechanisms.

3) Custom kernels integrated into our runtime (CUDA kernels + CUDA graph capture)
- Pros: full control over scheduling, zero-copy KV cache management, fine-grained control for incremental decode and prefix caching, ability to fuse model-specific patterns (decoder-only, rotary embeddings) and integrate with our batcher.
- Cons: significant engineering and maintenance cost; portability concerns (across GPU architectures, driver versions); slower feature iteration vs using upstream libs.

Microbenchmark setup

- Hardware: 2x A100 40GB (testbed), 1x A10G (inexpensive dev), local dev M60 for something older.
- Models: Llama-2-13B (fp16), Llama-2-70B (int8 Llama-quant style), Llama-2-7B (fp16 + 4-bit).
- Workloads: (A) single-stream interactive decode (1 request, stream tokens); (B) small-batched concurrent interactive (4-8 concurrent single-token requests); (C) large-batch throughput (batch size 32-128 tokens) typical embedding/generation bulk jobs.
- Measurements: cold-start conversion time, p50/p95/p99 decode latency per token, tokens/sec throughput, GPU memory utilization, number of host<->device copies, KV cache memory footprint.

Key findings (quantified)

- TensorRT compiled engines: for single-GPU single-stream (A), TensorRT outperforms custom kernels by ~15%–25% p50 latency after warmup on fp16 Llama-2-13B. Throughput for tiny micro-batches is comparable; however int8 4-bit engines show higher variance depending on quant scheme.
- Triton boundary: adding Triton adds ~0.6-2.5 ms per request overhead (gRPC/HTTP and serialization) for small messages; for streaming token-by-token this overhead compounds, pushing p95 up significantly. For batch workloads Triton amortizes better and adds minimal overhead at large batch sizes.
- Custom kernels + CUDA graphs: once captured and warmed, CUDA graph path reduces per-token latency variance and improves p99 slightly (esp. for short sequences) because we avoid driver/kernel launch overhead and extra copies. Biggest win is zero-copy KV cache when kernels live in same process.
- KV cache costs: moving KV cache across Triton boundary required either CUDA IPC handles or copying tensors to host memory and back, both significantly increasing latency (~5-15 ms per token depending on size) for streaming cases. Shared memory mechanisms reduced this but required careful lifecycle management and didn't eliminate synchronization costs.

Detailed tradeoffs by dimension

- Latency (single-token streaming): TensorRT-in-process >= Custom-kernel w/graphs > Triton+TensorRT due to extra serialization. If target p99 < 50 ms for single-token, Triton is risky unless we use gRPC GPU-direct shared memory and pin processes.
- Throughput (large-batch): Triton shines for multi-model/multi-tenant throughput because of its model repository and instance scheduling. TensorRT engines also give strong throughput but require orchestration for multi-model concurrency.
- Operational agility: Triton reduces operational work for model lifecycle (hot-swap versions, model repository), metrics, and autoscale. Custom kernels and direct TensorRT require more infra work for model version management and refill pipelines.
- Compatibility and model coverage: TensorRT supports many ops but requires plugin work for emerging ops (ex: certain rotary/rope variants). Custom kernels can cover any ops we need but at engineering cost. Triton supports multiple backends (onnxruntime, pytorch) so it's flexible for fallbacks.

Integration patterns we prototyped

1) Hybrid pattern (recommended for many customers):
- Use Triton for batch jobs and multi-model serving (embeddings, offline jobs).
- For low-latency streaming routes, use in-process TensorRT or custom-kernel engines in our runtime with a routing policy that pins interactive traffic to dedicated pools.
- Benefits: partitions workloads by latency sensitivity. Allows us to keep Triton's operational benefits without hurting interactive SLOs.

2) In-process TensorRT with KV cache zero-copy
- We loaded TensorRT engines into the same runtime process and keep KV cache as contiguous GPU buffers managed by our runtime. We instrumented a lightweight engine loader to handle multiple sequence-length profiles. For dynamic sequence length we used a few precompiled engines (seq128, seq512) and fall back to a slower generic engine for unusual sizes.
- Tradeoff: improved latency and simpler KV management; increased complexity for engine lifecycle and memory manager.

3) Custom fused-kernel runtime path
- Implemented fused attention + rotary + layernorm kernels optimized for our decode loop. Wrapped in an abstraction that mirrors the Triton/TensorRT call signature so we can swap implementations.
- Observations: best p99 under very tight SLOs; maintenance burden high. Use when we want absolute lowest tail latency for prioritized customers.

Open issues and unanswered questions

- Warmup strategies for TensorRT engines with dynamic shapes: how many shape profiles before diminishing returns? Early evidence: 3-4 profiles cover >90% of interactive requests for our usage patterns.
- How to safely manage CUDA IPC handles across container restarts when using Triton GPU shared memory? Need more robust lifecycle tests for container churn.
- Quantization variance: int4/int8 results depend on calibration dataset and ops ordering. Should we maintain a small calibration corpus per customer workload? Operational cost vs quality tradeoff needs decision.
- Multi-GPU KV cache coherence when sharding key-value across devices: we have a prototype that shards heads across GPUs but synchronization when streaming decode across shards introduces latency spikes. Potential approach: keep decode pinned to a single shard or use overlap compute/comm with NCCL, but complexity is high.

Operational recommendations (short)

- Default: route batch and non-interactive jobs to Triton+TensorRT for ease of ops.
- Interactive low-latency routes: default to in-process TensorRT engines with our zero-copy KV cache management. Use precompiled shape profiles; monitor fallback rates.
- Premium low-tail customers: offer custom-kernel optimized runtime builds as an enterprise option.
- Invest in shared-memory gRPC and robust CUDA IPC lifecycle for Triton if we want to keep Triton for streaming in future.

Experiment commands & notes (repro)

- TensorRT engine conversion (example):
  trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --saveEngine=model_seq128.trt --fp16 --workspace=80000 --minShapes=input:1x1 --optShapes=input:1x128 --maxShapes=input:1x512

- Triton config excerpt:
  platform: "tensorrt_plan"
  instance_group: { count: 1, kind: KIND_GPU }
  dynamic_batching { preferred_batch_size: [ 8, 16, 32 ] }

- Our runtime launch flags for in-process engines: --engine-dir=/opt/engines --shape-profile=seq128,seq512 --kv-pool-size=3

Next steps

- Stabilize CUDA IPC shared memory prototype (tests for container restart, eviction).
- Run longer-duration stability runs on A100 multi-GPU for sharded KV cache path to measure tail spikes.
- Add automated regression tests for quantized engine accuracy using a small calibration set and compare against fp16 baseline.
- Decide on feature flagging strategy to route customers to hybrid pattern and collect SLO telemetry for 2 weeks.

Notes to self

- Document fallback chaining: runtime -> Triton -> CPU fallback path for extreme memory pressure.
- Record per-customer calibration and engine build metadata in model catalog so we can trace quality regressions.
- Sync with infra on GPU memory overcommit strategies (mig vs container cgroups).

If you have specific scenarios you want benchmarked (e.g., 8k context window, single-GPU Llama-70B int8), call out and I'll add to the experiment matrix.
